Creating successful preventative and intervention plans requires an understanding of the many, multi-level factors that contribute to psychological discomfort. The objective of this scoping review was to use the Socio-Ecological Model (SEM) to map the determinants of psychological distress among college students in a comprehensive manner. Methods: A total of 15 review publi- cations published between 2015 and 2024, including narrative reviews, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and umbrella reviews, were analyzed under the guidance of PRISMA ScR. These studies synthesized evidence across various countries, including China, Iran, India, Canada, Egypt, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, and the United States. Results: Academic pressure, financial stress, poor sleep, unhealthy coping mechanisms, and pre-existing mental health issues were all individual-level concerns, with female and minority students being more vulnerable. Strong familial ties and friendships served as protective interpersonal support. Heavy academic workloads, strict grading guidelines, a lack of mental health resources, and unwelcoming campus environments were among the institutional factors. Stigma and socioeconomic disparities are examples of community-level variables that make mental health issues worse. Conclusions: Student mental health is shaped by interrelated factors across all SEM levels. Integrated, multi-level strategies are essential to fostering supportive campuses, strengthening community networks, and implementing inclusive policies that promote mental health equity. hits.text: Introduction Mental health disorders typically emerge in early adulthood (De Lijster et al., 2016) and rates can be especially high in college students (Eisenberg et al., 2013). A survey of 571 college campus counseling centers found that anxiety was the number one reason that students sought counseling (LiViness et al., 2017). Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health conditions reported among college students at 11.9% (Pedrelli et. al, 2015). Many college students likely experience inflated rates of anxiety, related to multiple aspects of collegiate life, such as increased responsibility, financial concerns, academic performance, and acceptance to graduate programs, with rates of anxiety and other disorders (e.g., depression) varying across discipline and class rank (Bieter et al., 2015; Lipson et al., 2016). Identifying students’ mental health disorders can result in earlier intervention and improve their chances of degree completion (Hunt et al., 2010). For students with anxiety, using a self-report questionnaire may be the first step in identifying a problem and encouraging them to seek treatment. Self-report questionnaires allow for both professionals and nonprofessionals to identify a probable disorder and assess the severity of symptoms. Ideally, such questionnaires are brief, accurate, and easy to administer. Many are available online and can be done quickly, privately, and remotely. The GAD-7 is a seven-item questionnaire used as a screening tool for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and as a measure for anxiety symptom severity.
